newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Global telecom pact said waiting on US decision.
newsitem.headline: Global telecom pact said waiting on US decision.

text.p: Trade negotiators said on Friday the fate of a global pact to open up basic telecommunications to world-wide competition lay in the hands of the United States and a decision could come from Washington late on Friday.

A key meeting at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to assess state of play in the talks was put back by five hours from 2.30 p.m. (1330 GMT) to 7.30 (1830 GMT) to give more time for the U.S. administration to consider its stance, one said.

"It's all up the Americans now. Everyone else is on board," said one diplomat closely involved in the negotiations -- which face a deadline of midnight in Geneva (2300 GMT) on Saturday for completion.

WTO analysts say a deal will quickly slash the cost of telephone calls for ordinary people and for businesses in every corner of the globe by injecting competition into what have long been government monopoly markets.
They say it will also boost the development of information technology industries, making the use of communications networks much cheaper.
WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero, who has made achievement of a telecoms deal his top priority, argues that it will also give a major impetus to development in the world's poorest countries.

Other negotiators said the U.S. administration -- under pressure from some key figures in Congress over its open trade policies -- had to make a political decision on whether to accept a package that did not meet all its targets.

The situation appeared similar to that in April last year when other participants in the effort to open up the booming global industry also felt a deal could be cut -- but the United States walked away saying not enough was on the table.

Many trade envoys argue it would be more difficult for Washington -- vital to a deal as it governs the world's biggest telecoms market -- to sink the pact a second time because many more countries had now made offers to open up.

They say support is much stronger this time from U.S. firms in the sector, who now see better prospects than they did last April for building up their business in developing countries as well as in Japan and the European Union.

A Canadian negotiator said his country, targetted by the United States for seeking to keep majority national ownership of telecoms firms, would be making a revised offer later in the day -- relating to access to satellite services.
"A good package is taking shape in the talks, and this has encouraged us to make an extra effort to get an agreement finalised," the official told Reuters.

But U.S. officials in Geneva declined any comment on whether intensive bilateral talks -- in which Washington was said to have been putting heavy pressure on key countries for better offers -- had eased prospects for a Washington go-ahead.
Throughout the week, they have repeated that current packages on the table from some important players had to be improved for a deal to be possible.

As the negotiations moved to a finale, the United Nations' International Telecommunications Union (ITU) issued a report predicting total world revenues from the industry could almost double by the year 2000 if a pact was reached.
It said total revenues for 1996 were some $800 billion, up $200 billion on 1995. By the turn of the century, the ITU declared, the annual figure could be $1,2 trillion.
